logic noun

also logical, logically, the logic of it, it doesn’t follow, logician

classical

Cic. Ac. 2.91; Cic. Fin. 2.15 (Lewis & Short)
M-O s.v. logic

dialectica, dialecticae f.

noun, first declension · Declension on Wiktionary

logic, the art of reasoning

Cicero’s and Quintilian’s word for the part of philosophy that deals with argument (Greek λογική); also in the Greek form dialecticē. A logician is dialecticus. For the logic of a particular argument or plan, “its reasoning”, Latin says ratiō (see reason).

Other words

  • cōnsentāneus, cōnsentānea, cōnsentāneum — logical, consistent (with something)

    adjective, with the dative · also used · classical · Cic. Off. 3.20: fōrmula Stōicōrum ratiōnī disciplīnaeque maximē cōnsentānea (Lewis & Short); M-O s.v. logical (ratiōnī cōnsentāneus) · Declension on Wiktionary

    In agreement with something, fitting; ratiōnī cōnsentāneus is “logical”, and cōnsentāneum est “it is logical, it follows”.

  • logica, logicae f. — logic

    noun, first declension · also used · late Latin · Isid. Orig. 2.22.1 (Lewis & Short) · Declension on Wiktionary

    Cicero writes the word in Greek letters (Fin. 1.22); in Latin letters it is late. dialectica is the classical word.

Examples

  • Nōn sequitur.

    That’s not logical (it doesn’t follow).Traupman 257

See also reason, argument, premise, assumption.
